weaknesses: Algorithm 4 is not well-defined at its first iteration: λ⁰ is the reciprocal square root of an empty sum and is therefore infinite/undefined. The proofs nevertheless include the t=0 term and incorrectly lower-bound its empty denominator by L⁰∞. Moreover, L⁰∞ depends on x¹, which itself requires the undefined first step. This directly undermines the central ALIAS algorithm and Theorems 2–3.

The Option-II proof derives dependence on f(x⁰)−f̃, but the theorem replaces this with Δ*=f(x⁰)−f(x*) using only f̃≤f(x*). The former can be arbitrarily larger than Δ*, so the stated complexity does not follow.

The stochastic and distributed bounds contain a non-vanishing variance-dependent error floor, yet the theorems claim finite complexity for reaching arbitrary ε. A bound of the form A/√T+B cannot imply the reported complexity without requiring ε>B and depending on ε−B. The SOS stochastic theorem is also internally inconsistent about whether growing mini-batches are used and ignores their quadratic total oracle cost.

SOS is not operationally parameter-free as stated: its required lower and upper search bounds, including k, depend on unknown Δ*, L∞, and gradient quantities. No adaptive outer search is supplied; Algorithm 2 can simply return infinity when the unknown upper-bound condition fails.

The practically strongest method, Algorithm 5, has no convergence analysis, requires an external γᵗ (fixed at 10⁻³ or combined with a cosine schedule), and contains an undefined β in its momentum update. Consequently, the headline deep-learning results do not validate the analyzed parameter-free algorithm.

The empirical evidence is insufficient for the small claimed improvements: no seeds, error bars, or significance estimates are reported. The LLaMA advantage is only 0.005 validation loss and the Swin advantage is 0.276 accuracy points, both plausibly within run-to-run variation. Hyperparameter-budget fairness is unclear, and the strongest ALIAS variant itself uses a cosine scheduler.

Reproducibility is poor because the promised code URL is blank and important initialization and tuning details—particularly d⁻¹/d⁰ and the undefined first ALIAS step—are missing. Table 1 also duplicates the same Sign-SGD label for apparently different schedules.

Despite the title and claimed multi-node contribution, there are no distributed experiments, communication measurements, or scaling results. The theory assumes convex smooth objectives, whereas the headline experiments use non-convex networks and an unanalyzed momentum variant.

Novelty appears incremental relative to the cited bisection, D-adaptation, Prodigy, and directional-smoothness approaches, while several relevant learning-rate-free baselines are absent. Given the fundamental algorithmic and theorem-level problems, the central claims are not technically supported.
